**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 3 (0790), Paper 3 (Problem-Solving and Analysis), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing THREE questions from Section One and ONE question from Section Two. Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION ONE: LOGIC**

*Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow:*

> The question of politics and good governance has awaken the spirit of philosophers and students of philosophy. This is because all philosophy students are disciplined persons. During a year of elections, especially presidential election, the general population receive messages of falsehood and propaganda from politicians. An intellectual affirmed: "if politicians conserve power through lies telling then the state would be governed by corrupt officials and if the general public lacks what it takes to detect lies telling, then the destiny of the state lies in the hands of incompetent leaders."
>
> However, it is either the state is ruled by the present ruling party or opposition party takes over power. One of the militants of the opposition party exclaimed "oh the presidential candidate of the present ruling party cannot govern our state on the basis that he has a questionable character and besides, a majority of the militants of the ruling party exhibit a long history of corrupt practices. Isolating philosophers from discussions regarding politics and good governance, is the most serious blunder most societies have committed and are still committing."

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify a suitable categorical proposition from the passage and state its subaltern. (1 mark)
(ii) Using a(i) above determine the contradictory of its obverse. (2 marks)
(iii) Given a(ii) above is true, what is the truth value of its contrary, contradictory and sub-contrary respectively? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A categorical proposition and its subaltern.**

A suitable categorical proposition is the universal affirmative (A) proposition taken from the passage:

**All philosophy students are disciplined persons.** (All $S$ are $P$, with $S$ = philosophy students and $P$ = disciplined persons.)

The subaltern of an A proposition is the I proposition with the same subject, predicate and quality, but particular:

**Some philosophy students are disciplined persons.**

**(ii) The contradictory of its obverse.**

Obversion keeps the subject, changes the quality of the proposition and replaces the predicate by its complement.

- Obverse of the A proposition: **No philosophy students are non-disciplined persons** (an E proposition).
- The contradictory of an E proposition is the I proposition (opposite quality and opposite quantity). So the contradictory of the obverse is:

**Some philosophy students are non-disciplined persons.**

This is logically equivalent to "Some philosophy students are not disciplined persons", the O proposition that contradicts the original A proposition: this is the expected result, because a proposition and its obverse are equivalent.

**(iii) Truth values, given that a(ii) is true.**

a(ii) is an I proposition ("Some $S$ are non-$P$"), assumed true. Using the traditional square of opposition:

| Relation | Proposition concerned | Truth value |
|:-|:-|:-:|
| Contrary | An I proposition has no contrary (contrariety holds only between A and E). The related universal A proposition of the same terms, "All philosophy students are non-disciplined persons", the superaltern of a(ii), cannot be derived from it | Doubtful (undetermined) |
| Contradictory | "No philosophy students are non-disciplined persons" (E) | **False** |
| Sub-contrary | "Some philosophy students are not non-disciplined persons" (O) | Doubtful (undetermined) |

Reason: an I proposition and an E proposition cannot be true together and cannot be false together, so the contradictory is false. Two sub-contraries can both be true but cannot both be false; knowing that one is true leaves the other open.

**Answer:** contrary: not applicable / doubtful; contradictory: false; sub-contrary: doubtful.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify a suitable disjunctive proposition from the passage above. (1 mark)
(ii) Use the disjunctive proposition to construct a valid Modus Tollendo Ponens and Modus Ponendo Tollens. (3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A disjunctive proposition.**

"**Either the state is ruled by the present ruling party or the opposition party takes over power.**" Let $R$ = the state is ruled by the present ruling party and $O$ = the opposition party takes over power. The proposition is $R \vee O$.

**(ii) The two disjunctive syllogisms.**

*Modus Tollendo Ponens* (by denying, it affirms): one disjunct is denied, the other is affirmed.

> Either the state is ruled by the present ruling party or the opposition party takes over power.
> The state is not ruled by the present ruling party.
> Therefore, the opposition party takes over power.

Form: $R \vee O,\ \sim R\ \therefore\ O$. It is valid (checked with a truth table: no row makes both premises true and the conclusion false).

*Modus Ponendo Tollens* (by affirming, it denies): one disjunct is affirmed, the other is denied. It is valid only when the disjunction is read in the exclusive sense "either... or... but not both", which is the natural sense here, since the state cannot at the same time remain in the hands of the ruling party and be taken over by the opposition.

> Either the state is ruled by the present ruling party or the opposition party takes over power (and not both).
> The state is ruled by the present ruling party.
> Therefore, the opposition party does not take over power.

Form: $(R \vee O) \cdot \sim(R \cdot O),\ R\ \therefore\ \sim O$. Valid (checked by truth table). With an inclusive "or" the same pattern would be the fallacy of affirming a disjunct.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify a suitable major premise for a complex destructive dilemma in the passage above. (1 mark)
(ii) Using c (i), construct a complex destructive dilemma. (3 marks)
(iii) Refute c (ii) by "taking it between the horns." (3 marks)

(The paper prints four mark labels for these three parts: 1 mark, 3 marks, 3 marks, 3 marks.)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) A suitable major premise.**

The intellectual's statement in the passage is a conjunction of two conditional propositions, which is exactly the major premise of a complex dilemma:

"**If politicians conserve power through lies telling then the state would be governed by corrupt officials, and if the general public lacks what it takes to detect lies telling, then the destiny of the state lies in the hands of incompetent leaders.**"

Symbols: $P$ = politicians conserve power through lies telling; $C$ = the state is governed by corrupt officials; $L$ = the general public lacks what it takes to detect lies telling; $I$ = the destiny of the state lies in the hands of incompetent leaders. Major premise: $(P \supset C) \cdot (L \supset I)$.

**(ii) The complex destructive dilemma.**

A dilemma is *complex* when the two conditionals have different antecedents and different consequents, and *destructive* when the minor premise denies (destroys) the consequents.

> If politicians conserve power through lies telling then the state would be governed by corrupt officials, and if the general public lacks what it takes to detect lies telling, then the destiny of the state lies in the hands of incompetent leaders.
> Either the state is not governed by corrupt officials or the destiny of the state does not lie in the hands of incompetent leaders.
> Therefore, either politicians do not conserve power through lies telling or the general public does not lack what it takes to detect lies telling.

Form: $(P \supset C) \cdot (L \supset I),\ \sim C \vee \sim I\ \therefore\ \sim P \vee \sim L$.

It is valid: if $\sim C$ is true, modus tollens on $P \supset C$ gives $\sim P$; if $\sim I$ is true, modus tollens on $L \supset I$ gives $\sim L$. (Confirmed with a 16-row truth table: no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false.)

**(iii) Refutation by "taking it between the horns".**

The two "horns" are the two alternatives of the disjunctive minor premise ($\sim C$ and $\sim I$). To take the dilemma between the horns is to deny the minor premise by showing that **neither alternative is true**, that is, that both $C$ and $I$ are true:

> It is false that either the state is not governed by corrupt officials or its destiny does not lie in the hands of incompetent leaders: in a country where politicians keep power by lies, the state is in fact governed by corrupt officials **and** its destiny does lie in the hands of incompetent leaders.

The minor premise $\sim C \vee \sim I$ is then false, so the dilemma, although valid, is unsound and does not prove that politicians do not lie or that the public is not deceived. (This differs from *grasping the dilemma by the horns*, which would deny one of the conditionals of the major premise, for example by arguing that conserving power through lies need not lead to corrupt officials where institutions are strong.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State the fallacy clearly committed in the passage. (1 mark)
(ii) Explain how it has been committed. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The fallacy:** argumentum **ad hominem** (an attack on the person), here in its abusive form combined with guilt by association.

**(ii) How it is committed.** The militant of the opposition party says that the presidential candidate of the ruling party "cannot govern our state" because "he has a questionable character" and because many militants of his party "exhibit a long history of corrupt practices". He does not examine the candidate's programme, competence or record in office: he attacks the man and his associates instead of the claim. A person's character, or the conduct of other members of his party, is not a logically sufficient reason for concluding that he cannot govern, so the conclusion does not follow from the reasons given.
